newsitem.title: TAIWAN: U.S. House chief Gingrich in Taiwan, meets Lee.
newsitem.headline: U.S. House chief Gingrich in Taiwan, meets Lee.

text.p: U.S. congressional chief Newt Gingrich met Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui on Wednesday, getting a red-carpet welcome after saying U.S. forces would defend the Nationalist-ruled island against attack by communist China.
"I'm glad to be here," Gingrich told Lee as the men shook hands in Lee's office.

The visit by Gingrich, the first House of Representatives speaker to come here since Washington switched diplomatic ties to Beijing in 1979, put an intense spotlight on Taiwan-China frictions, seen by Beijing as a key irritant in Sino-U.S. ties.
The state-run Central News Agency said Gingrich and Lee were expected to discuss the complicated relations between the United States, China and Taiwan during their closed-door talks.

China, which had hosted Gingrich at the weekend, warned the United States on Tuesday not to interfere in Beijing's dealings with Taiwan, saying Washington should desist from large-scale high-technology weapons sales to Taipei.

Gingrich's arrival brought the rare sight of a U.S.-flagged military plane emblazoned with "United States of America" landing at a Taipei military base, something that was common between 1949 and 1978 when Taiwan enjoyed close official ties.
Gingrich shook hands warmly with Foreign Minister John Chang and leaders of Washington's de facto embassy, the private but government-funded American Institute in Taiwan.
He made no comment to reporters but was expected to hold a news briefing after meeting Lee and lunching with Vice President Lien Chan. His entire visit was to last just three hours.
Chang hailed the visit as crucial for Taiwan's exiled Republic of China government, which has been trying to break out of a diplomatic isolation imposed by Beijing.
"This is an extremely significant affair," Chang told reporters at the airport just before Gingrich arrived.
"This shows that the Republic of China is an indispensable facet of the United States policy in Asia," he said.
Taiwan and China split after a civil war ended in 1949 and the island has diplomatic ties with just 30 countries -- mostly underdeveloped states in Africa and Latin America.

Gingrich said after his weekend Beijing visit that he had told China's communist leader that U.S. forces would defend Taiwan in the face of attack by Beijing -- something Washington has not explicitly promised to do.
Despite subsequent attempts by the White House to play down Gingrich's comments, Chang contended that the outspoken speaker's stance accorded with the official U.S. position.
"I think the positions of the U.S. legislative branch and the executive branch regarding policies toward Taiwan are the same, even if they choose to use different languages," Chang said.
Beijing, which opposes contacts between Taiwan's leaders and U.S. officials, briefly downgraded its U.S. ties after President Lee was allowed to make a private U.S. visit in mid-1995.
China has regarded Taiwan as a renegade province since a civil war split them in 1949 and vows to attack if it declares independence.
It opposes U.S. arms sales to the island as interference in China's internal affairs.
U.S. law authorises Washington to offer defensive arms to Taiwan but is ambiguous on whether the United States would come to the Nationalist-ruled island's defence.
